newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU approves German, French EMU plans - source.
newsitem.headline: EU approves German, French EMU plans - source.

text.p: European Union finance ministers on Monday approved German and French economic convergence plans, aimed at bringing their economies into line for the start of European monetary union, a delegation source said.
"They have approved the(German)plan. There was only a short discussion," the source said. He later said the French plan had also been approved.
The ministers, facing mounting speculation of a delay to the planned launch of a common currency, had been considering the credibility of the two country's monetary union plans.

Their meeting comes amid record unemployment in Germany, Europe's economic powerhouse, and doubts over whether Bonn itself could strictly adhere to the budgetary rigours outlined in the Maastricht treaty.
Specifically, the ministers analysed the economic convergence plans of both Germany and France.
"It is a convincing document," said Luxembourg prime minister and finance minister Jean-Claude Juncker when asked by reporters about Germany's plan.
"But it shows all the difficulties Germany and others may have to fulfill the criteria," he added.

With the number of jobless in Germany totalling close to 4.8 million, analysts and EU monetary officials had begun to question whether additional spending cuts are needed to meet the country's ambitious deficit target of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
A report in a leading German magazine over the weekend suggested that an estimate in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office put the 1997 deficit at 4.15 percent of GDP.
Bonn officials strongly denied such a forecast existed.

Apart from the expected struggle Germany will have in meeting the Maastricht deficit target of three percent of output, the government's level of outstanding public debt has also been troublesome, moving up above the 60 percent of GDP reference value.

Speaking to reporters ahead of the meeting, German finance minister Theo Waigel cited several reasons behind the debt increase, including large transfers to eastern Germany and central European states.
EU officials confirmed on Friday that Bonn's expectation for total debt is 61.5 percent of GDP, up from 60.7 percent in 1996.
Details of Bonn's convergence plans also include the relatively optimistic assumption that unemployment in 1997 will not exceed an average of 4.1 million.
Among the other assumptions in the 1997 German plan is 2.5 percent real GDP growth, a rise in inflation of 1.5 percent and a 6.2 percent yield on long-term government bonds.
Several finance ministers, including Ireland's Rauiri Quinn, rejected any speculation over which countries might not qualify for the single currency.
"Any speculation about the outcome of anyone's economic performance will have to wait until the actual results," Quinn told reporters.
Countries wishing to join monetary union will be judged on their 1997 economic performance, the details of which will not be known until early next year.
The French programme, which includes a 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP target, sees outstanding government debt slightly below 60 percent of output.
Separately, the ministers will consider financial assistance to Albania in order to stabilise the country's political situation, diplomats said.
